name: Opera Mauve
lede: Opera Mauve is a dusty pink-purple whose own name is uncertain: the 1930 plate it comes from scanned so poorly that two dictionaries read it two different ways.

sections.title: A name two dictionaries disagree on
sections.body:
*Mauve* is the French word for the mallow flower, lent to color language in 1856 for mauveine, William Perkin's first aniline dye [1]. Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary lists a mauve at plate 42, row H5, which our library dates to a first use of 1927; the plate's scanned print is damaged enough that its optical character recognition read the name as "Jpera Mauve" [2]. The ISCC-NBS committee matched that garbled reading to "era Mauve" in its own 1955 dictionary, while our library's working name for the same plate cell is "Opera Mauve"; books disagree on which reading is right, and neither is certain [2][3].

The plate's near neighbor at F4, "Morning Glory" from 1920, suggests the whole block was a cluster of flower-toned mauves [2]. The nearest look-alikes on file are [[dusty-lavender]] and [[cosmos]], both close by, and [[heather|Heather]], a touch purpler [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: A close match to this mauve appears in only 7 of our 23,781 archived paintings, about 0.03 per cent, with the within-painting lens finding it in just 1; that makes it rarer than 88 per cent of our named colors [5]. The sample is too small here to support any claim about when or where it is most common, and the count is as photographed, a screen-color match rather than a pigment test [5].

origin.named_after: mauve (French for mallow) + a disputed reading of its 1930 dictionary plate cell, "Opera" or "era"
origin.source: Maerz & Paul, A Dictionary of Color (1930)

disambiguation.gloss: a different, more saturated mauve on our library, not the same plate cell

questions.q: Why is there disagreement over whether this color is called "Opera Mauve" or "era Mauve"?
choices: The scanned 1930 dictionary plate is damaged, and its text reads ambiguously
Two different flowers inspired two different names
Crayola and ISCC-NBS each trademarked a different name
The color changed between two printings of the same book
